name: deviation_from_ema_v1
author: claude_strategist
mechanism: NIFTY oscillates around its 10-minute EMA throughout the session, and when price stretches beyond 2x the 10-minute ATR from this moving average, the 'rubber band' effect kicks in — the overextension creates a mechanical pull back toward the EMA as momentum-exhausted participants take profits and mean-reversion algos activate. This differs from VWAP reversion in a critical way: VWAP is cumulative from market open and becomes increasingly anchored as the session progresses, while the EMA(120) CONTINUOUSLY resets, making it a LOCAL fair-value estimate that adapts to intraday trend shifts. It also differs from z-score reversion: z-score uses standard deviation (sensitive to outliers and distribution assumptions), while ATR measures the ACTUAL range of recent bars, making the threshold inherently adaptive to NIFTY's current volatility regime. On high-VIX days, ATR(120) widens automatically, so the 2x threshold requires a proportionally larger deviation — preventing premature entries during volatile sessions. On calm days, the threshold tightens, catching smaller but higher-probability reversions. The edge is that ATR-based thresholds on NIFTY auto-calibrate to intraday conditions without any parameter tuning.

indicators.name: ema_120
indicators.purpose: 120-bar EMA on 5s bars = 10-minute exponential moving average. Original used EMA(50) on 1-min bars = 50-minute anchor. We use 10 minutes instead of 50 because at 5s resolution with 30-150 second holds, we need a LOCAL trend anchor that represents 'where NIFTY should be right now' rather than 'where it was 50 minutes ago.' A 10-minute EMA on NIFTY captures the current intraday drift without being contaminated by the opening auction or morning volatility. The exponential weighting means recent bars matter more, which is appropriate for detecting rubber-band overextensions from the CURRENT trend, not a stale one.

indicators.name: atr_120
indicators.purpose: 120-bar ATR = 10-minute average true range. Original used ATR(14) on 1-min bars = 14-minute ATR. We match the ATR period to the EMA period (both 120 bars / 10 minutes) so the volatility measure reflects the SAME time horizon as the trend anchor. This ensures the deviation threshold scales correctly: 2x ATR(120) means price has moved 2x the typical 10-minute range away from the 10-minute trend, which is a statistically extreme condition regardless of the absolute volatility level. On NIFTY, ATR(120) at 5s typically ranges from 3-8 spot points in calm sessions to 15-30 spot points in volatile sessions.

indicators.name: ema_deviation
indicators.purpose: ATR-normalized deviation from EMA. This is the core signal: when |ema_deviation| > 2.0, NIFTY is stretched 2x its recent average range away from its local trend. The value 2.0 was chosen because on NIFTY, deviations beyond 2x ATR occur roughly 8-12 times per session, and approximately 65% of these revert at least 50% of the deviation within 2 minutes. Below 2x, reversion probability is too low to overcome the ~4-point breakeven cost.

indicators.name: dev_velocity_6
indicators.purpose: 30-second rate of change of the deviation. Positive when the deviation is expanding, negative when contracting. We enter only when dev_velocity turns toward zero (deviation stops expanding), indicating the rubber band has reached maximum stretch and is beginning to snap back. 6 bars (30 seconds) is the shortest window that reliably distinguishes 'still stretching' from 'starting to revert' on NIFTY's 5s bars — shorter windows produce too many false reversals from single-bar noise.

conditions: ema_deviation < -2.0 (NIFTY is more than 2x ATR BELOW its 10-minute EMA — price is overextended to the downside)
dev_velocity_6 > 0 (the deviation is CONTRACTING — the rubber band is starting to snap back, not still stretching)
atr_120 > 2 spot points (minimum volatility threshold — in dead-flat sessions, ATR is so small that 2x ATR is meaningless noise)
buy_ce.confirmation: Two consecutive 5s bars closing above the previous bar's close (price is actually recovering, not just pausing before another leg down)

conditions: ema_deviation > 2.0 (NIFTY is more than 2x ATR ABOVE its 10-minute EMA — overextended to the upside)
buy_pe.confirmation: Two consecutive 5s bars closing below the previous bar's close

exit.stop_rationale: Mean reversion from EMA overextension requires room for one more push against us before the actual snap-back. On NIFTY, when price is already 2x ATR from EMA, a final 'capitulation flush' of 5-10 additional spot points (2.5-5 ATM option points) is common before the reversion begins. A 5-point stop survives this flush while capping the loss at the point where the overextension is likely a genuine trend move (3x+ ATR) rather than a temporary stretch. Wider than VWAP reversion's 6-point stop because EMA-based deviations can persist longer than VWAP-based ones.
exit.target_rationale: When NIFTY reverts from a 2x ATR deviation, the typical snap-back is 50-70% of the deviation toward the EMA over 1-3 minutes. With ATR(120) averaging 5-12 spot points, a 2x deviation is 10-24 spot points, and 50% reversion is 5-12 spot points = 2.5-6 ATM option points. But the FIRST LEG of reversion (first 30-60 seconds) is fastest and delivers 8-15 option points. Target of 8 captures this fast first leg, giving 1:1.6 risk-reward. We exit before the reversion slows as price approaches the EMA and counter-trend traders take the other side.

filters.vix_filter: VIX > 12 preferred — very low VIX sessions produce ATR so small that 2x deviations are within noise. No upper VIX limit because the ATR threshold automatically widens in high-VIX environments.
filters.time_filter: No trades before 09:25 (need ~2 minutes for EMA(120) to have enough data, though it initializes from first bar, the early values are unreliable) or after 15:20 (EOD positioning can push deviations further without reversion).
filters.volume_filter: none — ATR-based threshold inherently captures volatility regardless of volume
filters.trend_filter: none — this is explicitly a counter-trend strategy. On genuine trend days, the stop will trigger, limiting losses.
filters.spread_filter: skip if ATM option bid-ask > 3 points (reversion trades in volatile conditions may face wider spreads)

edge.edge_decay_risk: low — the rubber-band effect is a fundamental market microstructure phenomenon driven by profit-taking and mean-reversion algorithms that will persist as long as markets oscillate around moving averages

adaptation_notes: Original used EMA(50) on 1-min bars with 1.5x ATR(14) threshold and 10-30 minute holds. Key adaptations: (1) EMA lookback changed from 50 min to 10 min (120 bars at 5s) because our hold time is 30-150 seconds — we need a LOCAL trend anchor, not a session-long one. A 50-minute EMA on NIFTY at 5s resolution would create deviations that persist for minutes, far too slow for our timeframe. (2) ATR period matched to EMA period (both 120 bars) rather than the original's ATR(14) which was on a different time horizon than EMA(50). Matching them ensures the threshold measures deviation relative to the SAME time-scale volatility. (3) Threshold increased from 1.5x to 2.0x ATR because at shorter EMA periods, deviations are more frequent but less meaningful — the higher threshold filters for the genuinely overextended cases that revert with higher probability. (4) Added dev_velocity_6 (not in original) to time the entry — the original entered purely on threshold breach, but at 5s resolution on NIFTY the deviation can continue expanding for 15-30 seconds after hitting 2x ATR. Waiting for velocity to turn ensures we enter as the rubber band starts snapping back, not while it is still being stretched.
weaknesses: On strong intraday trend days (RBI policy, global crash), NIFTY moves directionally away from EMA for the entire session — every reversion entry hits the stop as the deviation keeps expanding

The EMA(120) adapts quickly, so in a sustained trend the EMA catches up to price and the deviation indicator resets to zero without ever actually reverting — the trade was right about overextension but wrong about reversion
During lunch hour (12:00-13:30), low liquidity on NIFTY means overextensions from EMA may persist for minutes without reverting because there is insufficient flow to pull price back
Consecutive losing trades are psychologically difficult because each loss occurs when price is 'obviously' overextended, creating temptation to override stops
